Persistent Representational Misalignment
Induces Vision-Language Model Failures

Yonatan Gideoni\NoHyper ††thanks: Correspondence to yg@robots.ox.ac.uk. Code can be found at https://github.com/YonatanGideoni/persistent_repr_misalignment. Affiliation: University of Oxford    Yoav Gelberg Affiliation: University of Oxford    Tim G. J. Rudner Affiliation: University of Toronto    Yarin Gal Affiliation: University of Oxford
Abstract

Vision-language models (VLMs) fail at some tasks that are simple for humans—but why? We hypothesize that many such failures stem from VLMs’ difficulties translating between vision and language representations—a misalignment the Platonic Representation Hypothesis predicts should disappear with scale. This paper is composed of two parts: in the first, we show that existing vision and language representations are linearly unalignable. This misalignment is an inherent property of the data and hence expected to persist regardless of either scale or the alignment’s complexity. In the second, we demonstrate how this misalignment both leads to a predictably induced generalization failure and correlates with existing failure modes, where more representationally aligned VLM backbones accordingly exhibit fewer failures. Overall, these results imply representations will not become aligned simply given sufficient scale, providing evidence against a strong version of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

1 Introduction

Although vision and language models are considered superhuman on many tasks (He et al., 2015; Achiam et al., 2023), their multimodal counterparts exhibit some very simple failures. Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle identifying visual analogies (Yiu et al., 2024), matching semantically different but syntactically similar captions to images (Thrush et al., 2022), identifying simple geometric properties like whether two circles overlap (Rahmanzadehgervi et al., 2024), and counting atypical objects, e.g. the number of legs on a three-legged chicken (Vo et al., 2025). Humans outperform VLMs on all of these tasks.

What causes these failures and why they persist is generally unclear, with several linked observations. Vo et al. (2025) observe that VLMs can rely on their language component’s world knowledge (“chickens typically have two legs”) more than on what their vision backbones see, but do not discuss why this occurs. Testing why VLMs struggle with fine visuolingual retrieval, Diwan et al. (2022) speculate that it is due to misalignment between the visual and text representations.

A lack of representational alignment is surprising given some common beliefs in the field. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis states that sufficiently well trained models should converge to equivalent representations (Huh et al., 2024), with many works presuming or relying on such convergence (Tjandrasuwita et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Jha et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Bahng et al., 2025; He et al., 2025).

In this paper, we call the Platonic Representation Hypothesis into question and show implications thereof on existing models. To test whether vision and language representations converge, we develop a simple theoretical framework for when sets of representations are alignable (Section 3). We find that existing representations are unalignable due to underlying differences in the data, meaning alignment will likely not naturally emerge with scale. This misalignment predictably leads to an induced generalization failure in vision-language models, where a VLM fails to recognize a concept its vision and language backbones know if it does not appear in its paired finetuning data (Section 4). Moreover, representational alignment correlates with performance on the failure modes, where more aligned VLM backbones lead to VLMs which exhibit fewer failures (Section 5).

Altogether, these results support the conjecture that a diverse set of VLM failures likely stem from representational misalignment and will not be resolved solely by increasing model scale. This conjecture provides a joint cause for seemingly disjoint failure modes while explaining why the failures persist even in very capable models.

2 Relations Between Representations

In this section we discuss different ways in which sets of representations can be similar. While there are many existing notions (Sucholutsky et al., 2023), many are statements on whether the representations are equivalent or alignable. We now discuss what each of these mean and the relationships between different kinds of similarity, with additional related work in Appendix A.

There are two main ways in which different sets of representations can be equivalent. The first is functional equivalence, where two representations or models producing some representations are used for some task. For example, take two sets of word embeddings used for retrieval. In this case, the representations are equivalent if they perform comparably well and make the same mistakes, thereby being indistinguishable from a black-box perspective. A weaker but related form of equivalence is representational equivalence (Klabunde et al., 2025), where sets of representations are equivalent up to some transformation. Invariances to different transformations define different similarity kernels between representations, with most similarity kernels defining two representations as equivalent if they are the same up to some (constrained) linear transformation, perhaps with some additional normalization (Kornblith et al., 2019, section 4). Works like the Platonic Representation Hypothesis primarily discuss representational equivalence (Huh et al., 2024). Representational equivalence is likely, but not guaranteed, to result in functional equivalence – for the word embeddings, an orthogonal transformation over an entire space would not affect which words are retrieved as distances would be preserved, but more general transforms could lead to functional differences.

Representational equivalence is closely related to representational alignment. For typical generative VLMs, pretrained vision and language models are combined using an adapter that projects vision representations into the language model, thereby aligning the vision representations with the language token embeddings (Alayrac et al., 2022; Merullo et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023). For retrieval, language and vision representations are aligned by being projected into a shared representation space (Radford et al., 2021). Representations that are representationally equivalent are easy to align, as a linear map is often sufficient to map between them. More broadly, representations can be functionally alignable if given some training they can be used together to generalize over some task, where generalization is important as an adapter may just memorize training data. If the adapter is a simple linear map, as it often is for generative VLMs (Liu et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2023), functional alignment implies a degree of representational alignment, as the learned map aligns the representations. This is often used in model-stitching (Lenc and Vedaldi, 2015; Bansal et al., 2021; Csiszárik et al., 2021), where parts of one model are stitched to another using a trained linear layer, as a way to probe whether two models learn the same representations.11 1 This reasoning has some known caveats; see Smith et al. (2025).

In practice, both equivalence and alignment are not binary properties but fall on various spectrums and in some cases one can imply another. Typical relationships between equivalence and alignment are summarized in this diagram, where arrows represent “X implies Y” and “typically” means that counterexamples exist but are somewhat adversarial. Thus, two representations being representationally equivalent typically implies they are functionally equivalent as well.

This framework helps understand how different statements on representations relate to one another. For example, the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (Huh et al., 2024) asserts that representations in different modalities should be representationally equivalent and tests this by showing trends in representational alignment. Representational alignment typically implies representational equivalence, thereby supporting their claim. Throughout this paper we will show different forms of alignment or equivalence fail to hold, noting how one not holding rules out another, e.g. representations cannot be functionally aligned if they are functionally inequivalent.

3 Broken Conditions for Representational Alignment

In this section we derive the conditions for representations to be linearly alignable. Operationally, many alignment metrics like CKA quantify whether sets of representations are linearly alignable up to normalization, restricted to some subset of linear transformations (Kornblith et al., 2019). In Appendix B we formalize some of this intuition, showing how certain bounds on representational alignability accordingly bound some common representational similarity metrics.

A useful way to test for representational alignability is by considering how concepts are related in different representations (Dhimoïla et al., 2026). For example, over a decade ago Mikolov et al. (2013b) showed that word embeddings trained on different languages have similar relationships between the same sets of words, so a linear map is sufficient to translate between representations in different languages. In this case each word embedding defines how a concept, namely its word, is represented.

One very simple kind of relationship between concepts is analogies. More formally, let there be some analogy where AA is to BB as CC is to DD, e.g. king is to queen as man is to woman. The vision representation of a concept like “king” can be found by averaging the representations of many images of kings. All presented theorems are based on simple known lemmas in linear algebra, with proofs delegated to Appendix C. If vXv_{X} denotes some model’s representation of concept XX then we can formally define an analogy as follows.

Definition 3.1 (Concepts and analogies in representations).

The vector representing some concept XX is denoted as vXv_{X}. The analogy AA is to BB as CC is to DD (denoted A:B::C:DA:B::C:D) is said to exist for a model’s representations of these concepts if vA−vB=vC−vDv_{A}-v_{B}=v_{C}-v_{D}. The tuple representing an analogy is denoted as vA:B::C:D≔(vA,vB,vC,vD)v^{A:B::C:D}\coloneqq(v_{A},v_{B},v_{C},v_{D}). We assume no concept is represented by the zero vector.

In practice, the analogy would only be approximate, so vA−vB≈vC−vDv_{A}-v_{B}\approx v_{C}-v_{D}. Throughout this section, take V,WV,W to be two finite-dimensional inner product spaces, e.g. ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}. One can intuitively think of them as the representations of two different models, potentially from different modalities. For simplicity, all inner products are viewed as dot products, where ⟨v,w⟩=vT​w\braket{v,w}=v^{T}w, but the theorems equally hold regardless of the kind of inner product.

If there are enough corresponding analogies between two models then one might expect a linear map between their representations to exist, as the analogies enforce a linear structure. In practice, this is not the case.

Theorem 3.2 (Analogies are insufficient for a linear map to exist).

Let there be two sets of the same analogies in VV and WW, {vAi:Bi::Ci:Di}\{v^{A_{i}:B_{i}::C_{i}:D_{i}}\} and {wAi:Bi::Ci:Di}\{w^{A_{i}:B_{i}::C_{i}:D_{i}}\}. There exist sets of analogies such that there is no corresponding linear map T:V→WT:V\to W such that ∀i,X:T⁡(vXi)=wXi\forall i,X:T(v_{X_{i}})=w_{X_{i}}.

The following example is effectively a proof of this theorem.

Example 3.3 (Different information can lead to inconsistent mappings).

Observe the following analogies in ℝ1\mathbb{R}^{1} and ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, vA=[1],vB=[2],vC=[3],vD=[4]v_{A}=[1],v_{B}=[2],v_{C}=[3],v_{D}=[4] and wA=[11],wB=[21],wC=[32],wD=[42]w_{A}=\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}1\\ 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr],w_{B}=\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}2\\ 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr],w_{C}=\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}3\\ 2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr],w_{D}=\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}4\\ 2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]. Clearly, there is no linear transformation T⁡(vX)=wXT(v_{X})=w_{X} as 4​vA=vD4v_{A}=v_{D} but 4​wA≠wD4w_{A}\neq w_{D}. The diagram to the right illustrates this visually.

Example 3.3 can be equivalently interpreted as one representation having information that is missing in the other. Intuitively, the second index in the ww vectors could be some information that is irrelevant for the analogy but consistently exists, like a typical syntax in a sentence or different lighting in an image.

A stronger requirement, which does result in linear mappings, is that the different representations have the same similarity structure, akin to the case of Mikolov et al. (2013b) in machine translation (Smith et al., 2017). For representations with unit norm this means that the cosine similarity between concepts AA and BB is the same in both modalities, so vAT​vB=wAT​wBv_{A}^{T}v_{B}=w_{A}^{T}w_{B}. For example, this condition implies that the cosine similarity between an image of a cat and an image of a dog is close to the cosine similarity between the words “cat” and “dog”.

Definition 3.4 (Similarity structures).

Given a set of concept representations {vXi}i=1N\{v_{X_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{N}, the Gram matrix Gi​j≔vXiT​vXjG_{ij}\coloneqq v_{X_{i}}^{T}v_{X_{j}} is said to define the representations’ similarity structure. Two representations are said to have the same similarity structure if their Gram matrices are the same, so ∀i,j:vXiT​vXj=wXiT​wXj\forall i,j:v_{X_{i}}^{T}v_{X_{j}}=w_{X_{i}}^{T}w_{X_{j}}.

Interestingly, having the same similarity structure implies that under some similarity metrics, like CKA, these representations are equivalent.

Theorem 3.5 (Same similarities enable linear mappings).

Let VV and WW have corresponding sets of concept representations, {vXi}i=1N,{wXi}i=1N\{v_{X_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{w_{X_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{N}. If they have the same similarity structure then there exists a linear map T:V→WT:V\to W such that ∀i:T⁡(vXi)=wXi\forall i:T(v_{X_{i}})=w_{X_{i}}.

This theorem is stronger than required for a linear map to exist, as the resulting TT is an isometry, a map that preserves distances. Moreover, assuming the spaces have the same dimension, such a map would have an inverse, so it loses no information as it allows mapping back and forth between them. In the single modality setting Smith et al. (2017) construct such a map for translating between sets of word embeddings, showing that the different embeddings indeed have a similar similarity structure. Representations having different similarity structures, however, restricts which transformations can map between them.

Corollary 3.6 (Different similarity structures rule out isometric mappings).

Assume V,WV,W have corresponding sets of concept representations but different similarity structures. Thus, there cannot exist an isometric linear map T:V→WT:V\to W such that ∀i:T⁡(vXi)=wXi\forall i:T(v_{X_{i}})=w_{X_{i}}.

A weaker condition that results in generic linear maps is requiring a form of generalized analogies to exist in both modalities. For example, if vzebra=vhorse+vstripesv_{\text{zebra}}=v_{\text{horse}}+v_{\text{stripes}} then wzebra=whorse+wstripesw_{\text{zebra}}=w_{\text{horse}}+w_{\text{stripes}} as well.

Theorem 3.7 (Generalized analogies enable linear mappings).

Let VV and WW have corresponding sets of concept representations, {vXi}i=1N\{v_{X_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{N} and {wXi}i=1N\{w_{X_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{N}. A linear map TT such that ∀i:T⁡(vXi)=wXi\forall i:T(v_{X_{i}})=w_{X_{i}} exists if and only if for all sets of scalars ai∈ℝa_{i}\in\mathbb{R} if ∑iai​vXi=0\sum_{i}a_{i}v_{X_{i}}=0 then ∑iai​wXi=0\sum_{i}a_{i}w_{X_{i}}=0.

Note that any generalized analogy can be written as ∑iai​vXi=0\sum_{i}a_{i}v_{X_{i}}=0, e.g. in the case of vzebra=vhorse+vstripesv_{\text{zebra}}=v_{\text{horse}}+v_{\text{stripes}} by moving vzebrav_{\text{zebra}} to the right hand side. A natural but important corollary of this theorem is that regular analogies not holding results in generalized analogies not holding as well.

Corollary 3.8 (Generalized analogies result in and require regular analogies).

If the conditions of Theorem 3.7 hold then any regular analogy must exist in both VV and WW as well, so if vA:B::C:Dv^{A:B::C:D} is an analogy then so is wA:B::C:Dw^{A:B::C:D}. Moreover, any analogy existing only in VV but not in WW, so vA−vB=vC−vDv_{A}-v_{B}=v_{C}-v_{D} but wA−wB≠wC−wDw_{A}-w_{B}\neq w_{C}-w_{D}, violates the conditions of Theorem 3.7.

In practice, text and vision have neither the same similarity structure nor the same analogies, respectively violating the conditions of both Theorem 3.5 and Theorem 3.7. Note that, as Theorem 3.7 is both a necessary and sufficient condition, this implies there is no concept-preserving linear map between them. We first show that text and vision representations have a different similarity structure and then that they have different analogies.

3.1 Language and Vision Have Different Similarity Structures

Similarity between datapoints is typically measured using representations from semantic similarity models. When these representations are normalized the dot product between them corresponds to a cosine similarity. For text and vision to have the same similarity structure (as per Definition 3.4), thus fulfilling the conditions of Theorem 3.5, two images with a given cosine similarity should have captions with approximately the same cosine similarity as well.

In practice, visual and textual descriptions of the same scene can be similar in one modality but very different in another due to the different modalities having different information contents. Figure 1 gives some examples of image-caption pairs where, due to each modality containing different information, this occurs. All image-caption pairs are from the COCO training set. Cosine similarities are computed using DINOv3 base for the images and Sentence Transformers’ all-MiniLM-L12-v2 for the captions (Siméoni et al., 2025; Reimers and Gurevych, 2019). Caption representations are averages over all of an image’s caption variants in the dataset.

Pairs like those in Figure 1 occur with a non-negligible frequency. Their prevalence can be quantified by finding pairs for which the cosine similarity between the images differs substantially from that between their captions, with the absolute difference in their cosine similarities being above some large threshold (e.g. 0.4). For about 2% of COCO image/caption pairs, their cosine similarity difference exceeds this threshold.

To quantitatively measure whether the two representations have the same similarity structure, we empirically compare their cosine similarities. Formally, for models f1,f2f_{1},f_{2} outputting normalized vectors f1​(x),f2​(x)f_{1}(x),f_{2}(x), we define CosSimRMSE⁡(f1,f2)≔𝔼⁡[(f1​(x)T​f1​(y)−f2​(x)T​f2​(y))2]\operatorname{CosSimRMSE}(f_{1},f_{2})\coloneqq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[(f_{1}(x)^{T}f_{1}(y)-f_{2}(x)^{T}f_{2}(y))^{2}]}, where the expectation is over the dataset. CosSimRMSE tests the extent to which two representations have the same similarity structure as per Definition 3.4. Although here both models get as input some xx,

in general one model could get an image while the other gets the corresponding set of captions. We measure CosSimRMSERatio(f1,f2|g1,g2)≔CosSimRMSE⁡(f1,f2)CosSimRMSE⁡(g1,g2)\operatorname{CosSimRMSERatio}(f_{1},f_{2}|g_{1},g_{2})\coloneqq\frac{\operatorname{CosSimRMSE}(f_{1},f_{2})}{\operatorname{CosSimRMSE}(g_{1},g_{2})}, with g1,g2g_{1},g_{2} representing two models in the same modality that form some lower bound. As Table 1 shows, vision and text models have an approximately 3×3\times larger gap between one another than models in the same modality. CLIP models, despite being purposely trained to align their representations, exhibit only a slightly better degree of alignment likely due to this difference being inherent in the data.

Altogether, this section’s results show that Theorem 3.5’s condition does not hold, as vision and language have very different similarity structures. We now show that Theorem 3.7 also cannot hold, showing that typical vision and language representations are linearly representationally unalignable.

3.2 Language and Vision Have Different Analogies

To see whether vision and language representations exhibit the same analogies we use the text analogy dataset of Mikolov et al. (2013a). These include analogies like king:queen::man:woman and Paris:France::London:UK. To compare lingual to visual analogies, we construct a new dataset called VisLingA (for visual lingual analogies), containing images representing various concepts, see Appendix E for qualitative examples.22 2 VisLingA can be found at https://huggingface.co/datasets/YGideoni/VisLingA. VisLingA is constructed by downloading about 5-10 images for each concept in the text analogies dataset. Analogies containing words with too few images and analogies in the plural, present-participle, and adjective-to-adverb categories are discarded as they tend to contain different words with mostly the same pictures, e.g. “car” and “cars”. Images were downloaded from Wikimedia Commons and filtered to images in the public domain or with CC0/CC-BY copyright licenses, keeping creator metadata. The final dataset has 15,455 analogies containing 746 distinct concepts.

An analogy A:B::C:DA:B::C:D can be said to exist in a modality if the representation of B−A+CB-A+C is close to DD. Retrieval is done over the embeddings for all the concepts in the dataset, so representations exhibit a set of analogies if they have a low average rank or high accuracy. Vision embeddings are found by averaging all of a concept’s images’ representations.

Results. Figure 2 shows that while most analogies exist in text, far fewer are present in vision. All text embedding models have top-10 analogy retrieval accuracies above 75% while all vision models get below 45%. This is likely due to the inherent difficulty of capturing abstract concepts or certain nouns in images, like countries and cities. Thus, as vision and language models exhibit different analogies, Theorem 3.7 cannot hold.

4 Vision-Language Models Fail to Generalize Across Modalities

A functional test for whether vision and language representations are alignable is to see if they can generalize out-of-distribution. Out-of-distribution generalization is important as an adapter between representations can act as a lookup table without relying on any shared underlying structure. For example, Mikolov et al. (2013b) found that, due to similar languages having some shared structure, a linear map between English and Spanish can translate words not in the map’s training data. If English and Spanish had no shared structure then the linear map could only map from a word in English to its Spanish analogue, like a dictionary, without generalizing further. Thus, in some cases, representational misalignment directly causes a lack of generalization.

The multimodal analogue of machine translation would be to train a VLM as usual while omitting some concepts from its paired finetuning data, see Figure 3 (right). These concepts must be ones that the vision and language backbones recognize independently, as otherwise it would be surprising for the final VLM to suddenly recognize them. We discuss what it means for vision and language models to recognize or “know” of a concept in Appendix G. After training, the VLM’s generalization can be tested by querying whether it recognizes the held-out concepts.33 3 This test is inspired by a thought experiment known as Molyneux’s problem – briefly, could a blind person, upon regaining their sight, be able to visually distinguish what they previously only felt? If tested a few days after gaining their sight, the answer is, surprisingly, yes – see Held et al. (2011).

Setup. We train a series of small generative and retrieval VLMs and large generative VLMs while omitting a few concepts from their datasets. Specifically, for the small-scale settings, we train adapters between frozen ViT-B/16 (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) and GPT2-small (Radford et al., 2019) models for image captioning or retrieval, with Appendix F containing ablations and technical details.

For the large-scale setup, we train a LLaVA-1.5-7B model (Liu et al., 2023), with two important differences relative to how LLaVA is typically trained. First, for its second stage of training, we use low-rank adapters (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2022) instead of tuning the entire LLM to reduce the possibility of catastrophic forgetting. Second, LLaVA typically uses a CLIP vision backbone, which already received language supervision during its pretraining and is already multimodal. Instead, we use a ViT-L/16@384 model that is trained for ImageNet classification. This ViT only saw images during its pretraining and has the same number of parameters and tokens as the default vision backbone.

Concept filtering and detection. In all settings, the held-out concepts are filtered from the finetuning datasets, with details in Appendix H. Specific concepts were selected due to being simple, synonymless, and are verifiably known by the models (e.g., all are ImageNet classes, so an image classifier clearly recognizes them). To measure how well a model detects a held-out concept after training, we construct a new test set consisting of concept images. Images containing the concepts are selected by querying ImageNet data using a CLIP model and filtering the resulting examples manually, yielding ∼\sim100 images per concept. For generation, a concept is detected if it appears in the generated answer, whereas for retrieval we benchmark the model on image-based text retrieval over 1000 prompts, one from each ImageNet class, including those of the held-out concepts.

Results. Table 2 shows that VLMs trained without the held-out concepts struggle to detect them compared to models trained on the regular full datasets. To ensure the models are properly trained, each section’s last row compares to a model trained elsewhere, showing they achieve similar performance. Figure 4 contains qualitative examples of descriptions generated by the LLaVA model trained without the held-out concepts.

For large-scale generation—although the LLaVA model trained without the concepts attains much worse performance than the one trained with them—it is still higher than the small-scale experiments’ accuracies. We speculate why this may be in Appendix J.

5 Representationally Aligned VLMs Exhibit Fewer Failures

The generalization failure described in the last section stems from representational misalignment. Representational misalignment is interesting in that, without explicit efforts to induce better alignment, misalignment should persist. As many VLM failures persist regardless of model scale, this raises the question whether additional failures may stem from representational misalignment as well (Diwan et al., 2022; Rahmanzadehgervi et al., 2024; Vo et al., 2025).

To test if representational alignment leads to fewer failures, we train 37 LLaVA models with different vision backbones and benchmark them on prediction tasks where VLM failures are common. All vision backbones use the same vision transformer architecture but have different pretraining objectives, such as image classification, multimodal contrastive losses, and so on. Thus, the only difference between models is the backbone’s resulting representations. For additional details see Appendix K.

To test whether improved representational alignment results in fewer failures we use the following datasets: Winoground measures matching accuracies between images with syntactically similar but semantically different captions (Thrush et al., 2022). VLMBias tests whether VLMs can count objects in counterfactual images (e.g., the number of legs on a three-legged chicken) (Vo et al., 2025). VLMBlind is a suite of simple geometric tasks like tracing paths in a simplified subway map (Rahmanzadehgervi et al., 2024). MMVP tests if a model can differentiate between pairs of images which are “CLIP-blind”, images which are similar per CLIP but dissimilar per other models (Tong et al., 2024).

Additionally, as a control, we test whether better representational alignment is correlated with better performance on datasets requiring the model to have properties orthogonal to representation alignment, such as reasoning. Bongard is a visual dataset consisting of geometric visual analogies that require reasoning about the relation between different sets of shapes (Wüst et al., 2024). OmniSpatial is a visual question answering spatial reasoning dataset (Jia et al., 2026).

Figure 5 shows that models with relatively higher representational alignment between their vision and language backbones tend to perform better on benchmarks that showcase VLM failures. Notably, Figure 5 (right column) shows that the correlation is not simply due to some vision backbones having better representations, as for the reasoning datasets the correlation is close to zero.

6 Discussion

In this paper we provide evidence that existing vision and language representations are linearly unalignable. Although these results are only over existing models, they are expected to hold regardless of model size due to the underlying reasons why the representations are misaligned. In Section 3, we find that the misalignment stems from the vision and language modalities having inherently different information; so what is similar in one may be dissimilar in another, and analogies may not carry over between modalities. As these differences are due to the data—not the models or training paradigm—they are expected to persist across all scales.

This implies that representations in different modalities should not converge—disproving a strong version of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis. Weaker versions of the hypothesis, where partial alignment is posited, can (and likely do) hold, consistent with prior work. Indeed, the weak trend in Figure 2 (left), where the vision models’ retrieval accuracy increases with scale, supports this conclusion.

A natural question is whether alignment is possible using more complex, nonlinear adapters between modalities. As the misalignment is due to the data, better adapters could not lead to alignment, as it is impossible for the adapter to regain lost information. For example, captioning a picture filled with a single color as “green” does not convey the color’s shade or hue.

More practically, representational misalignment has functional implications. We hypothesize that many noted VLM failure modes are due to representational misalignment, explaining why they persist in spite of continued improvements in model performance. The generalization failure demonstrated in Section 4 and the correlation between having fewer failures and representational alignment in Section 5 both support this hypothesis.

There are several caveats to our conclusions, with a broader discussion deferred to Appendix L. Most notably, our results only intervene in one direction – showing that representational misalignment can lead to failures – and do not yet show that fixing the misalignment directly reduces the failures. While there are some works which broadly show that better alignment leads to improved performance (Ma et al., 2024; Yamaguchi et al., 2025; Gan et al., 2026), finding a proper fix is an important avenue for future work. Moreover, although we show that representational alignment is linked to better results on datasets exhibiting VLM failures, this may only be a component and not the failures’ sole cause. Some failures likely stem from other causes, such as a lack of reasoning capabilities.

Ethics statement

We do not foresee any significant ethical consequences of this work. As far as we are aware, VisLingA does not contain concepts that would likely pose any safety risks. However, as it contains images from Wikimedia, it contains trace amounts of sensitive publicly available images, such as partial nudity and historical violence. Creator metadata for all images in VisLingA is kept, with only images in the public domain or with CC0/CC-BY copyright licenses being used.

Appendix A Related Work

Adding modalities can harm performance. The generalization failure and results on representational misalignment here demonstrate that when representations are unalignable then stitching them together leads to worse performance, expressed as a lack of generalization. While this work focuses on tasks with language outputs, Ramachandran et al. (2025) similarly find that state-of-the-art VLMs perform worse than vision-only models on standard vision tasks, although without interpreting why. Our work fills this gap.

A converse conclusion would be that removing modalities could improve generalization. This was observed, albeit not understood, in Goyal et al. (2025). Goyal et al. (2025) use a VLM for a robot’s vision-language-action model (VLA) without explicitly mapping into action-space, instead conveying actions as text. Their approach outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods that explicitly add the action modality.

There are cases when adding modalities would be expected to improve performance, but those likely require only in-distribution generalization. When the additional modalities enable training from large-scale data (Radford et al., 2021) or better supervision, e.g. using multi-task learning (Wang et al., 2025a), it is likely that in-distribution performance will improve.

Representational misalignment. Many works observe some form of multimodal representational misalignment, but often attribute it to a lack of scale (as would be expected per the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (Huh et al., 2024)) or do not interpret it; see Shu et al. (2025) for a survey. Notably, Liang et al. (2022) note there being a “modality gap” between vision and language representations in CLIP-like contrastive learning, attributing it not to the inherent information difference in the modalities but to model initialization and optimization. This viewpoint is contested (Udandarao, 2022), with Schrodi et al. (2025) arguing, similarly to this work, that the modality gap is due to inherent information differences in the data.

Several prior works note caveats to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis. Gröger et al. (2026) note that representations can seem to converge simply due to confounders, e.g. wider models can have higher representational similarity. The experiments in Section 5 are designed so all models have the same architecture, circumventing this pitfall. Li et al. (2024) speculate that some representations might be inherently unalignable, such as vision and language, with our work providing evidence this is indeed the case.

Analogies in representations. Analogies have been seen to exist in representations since the seminal work of Mikolov et al. (2013a), with many contemporary works assuming or relying on analogies in representations (Trager et al., 2023; Turner et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Piantadosi et al., 2024; Merullo et al., 2024). Analogies have been argued to arise due to concepts being represented as linear directions in representation spaces (“the Linear Representation Hypothesis”, (Park et al., 2024)). However, this viewpoint has some known limitations, especially when analogies are used for retrieval (Drozd et al., 2016; Rogers et al., 2017).

VLM failures. VLMs exhibit many simple failures, some of which are not analyzed here. Yuksekgonul et al. (2022) demonstrate instances where VLMs can act as bags-of-words and propose a contrastive learning method to mitigate this behaviour. Tong et al. (2024) demonstrate VLMs giving systematically wrong answers over certain curated visual question answering datasets, likely due to their CLIP vision backbones. They explore the design space of VLMs and propose changes that improve performance. Pawlonka et al. (2025) show that VLMs struggle perceiving fine-grained concepts in everyday real-world images. Khangaonkar et al. (2026) find that VLMs struggle detecting spatial inconsistencies between sets of images, e.g. a rotated chair. van Sprang et al. (2026) show that some reasoning inconsistencies likely arise due to representational misalignment, which could imply that the analysis in section 5 applies also to some reasoning tasks. Campbell et al. (2024) posit that various VLM failures are due to the binding problem, where models fail to associate together different features of an object.

Appendix B Bounds On Some Representational Alignment Metrics

In this appendix we show how if two sets of representations are linearly alignable only to some given extent then some representational alignment metrics are bounded in some sense by the degree of alignment. It is easiest showing these results when using different measures of linear alignability for different similarity metrics, due to how different similarity metrics measure different properties of the representations. However, any alignability metrics we use being zero implies the two representations are linearly alignable.

Notation. We first introduce some notation, mostly following that of Kornblith et al. (2019). Intuitively, given corresponding sets of representations Y∈ℝn×p1,X∈ℝn×p2Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p_{1}},X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p_{2}},44 4 Note we assume XX has at least as many features as YY while Kornblith et al. (2019) assume the opposite; this is purely notational but makes some proofs more intuitive later. XX is linearly alignable to YY if there exists a weight matrix W∈ℝp2×p1W\in\mathbb{R}^{p_{2}\times p_{1}} such that X​W=YXW=Y. XX is a matrix consisting of nn representations with p2p_{2} features, with YY being another such matrix but with p1p_{1} features. Following Kornblith et al. (2019), we assume that p1≤p2p_{1}\leq p_{2} and that X,YX,Y have been centred, or in other words, have zero mean over their columns.

CCA. Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) finds linear transformations that maximize the correlations between two sets of representations (Hotelling, 1992; Morcos et al., 2018). One similarity index given by CCA is Yanai’s GCD measure (Ramsay et al., 1984; Kornblith et al., 2019), which between XX and YY is RCCA2≔‖QYT​QX‖F2p1R^{2}_{\text{CCA}}\coloneqq\frac{||Q_{Y}^{T}Q_{X}||_{F}^{2}}{p_{1}}, where QY,QXQ_{Y},Q_{X} are matrices with orthonormal columns spanning the columns of YY and XX respectively.

CKA. Centred kernel alignment (CKA) is an extension of some prior representational similarity indices, which is notably invariant to orthogonal transformations but not to linear maps in general (Kornblith et al., 2019). Kornblith et al. (2019) showed that in many cases CKA better identifies intuitively corresponding representations than other similarity indices. Formally, CKA is defined as CKA≔‖YT​X‖F2‖XT​X‖F​‖YT​Y‖F\text{CKA}\coloneqq\frac{||Y^{T}X||_{F}^{2}}{||X^{T}X||_{F}||Y^{T}Y||_{F}}.

Limited linear alignability bounds CCA. Arguably the simplest alignability metric is l≔minW⁡‖Y−X​W‖F2l\coloneqq\min_{W}||Y-XW||_{F}^{2}, where l=0l=0 if there exists a weight matrix such that Y=X​WY=XW and is nonzero otherwise. Here we show how ll is bounded if X,YX,Y are not linearly alignable, and accordingly leads to a bounded CCA. Note that we do not assume X,YX,Y, or WW have any special form, beyond that XX has at least as many features as YY.

Note that YY decomposes into a matrix contained in XX’s column space and a matrix orthogonal to it. l=0l=0 if YY is wholly contained in XX’s column space, as then it is a linear combination of XX’s columns, in which case XX and YY are linearly alignable. More generally, denote by PXP_{X} a projection onto XX’s column space, such that Y=PX​Y+(I−PX)​YY=P_{X}Y+(I-P_{X})Y. Thus, note that l=minW⁡‖Y−X​W‖F2=minW⁡‖(I−PX)​Y+PX​Y−X​W‖F2l=\min_{W}||Y-XW||_{F}^{2}=\min_{W}||(I-P_{X})Y+P_{X}Y-XW||_{F}^{2}. As PX​Y−X​WP_{X}Y-XW is contained in XX’s columns while (I−PX)​Y(I-P_{X})Y is orthogonal to it, from Pythagoras’ theorem we have that l=‖(I−PX)​Y‖F2+minW⁡‖PX​Y−X​W‖F2=||(I−PX)​Y||F2l=||(I-P_{X})Y||_{F}^{2}+\min_{W}||P_{X}Y-XW||_{F}^{2}=||(I-P_{X})Y||_{F}^{2}, where the second term is zero as PX​YP_{X}Y is in the column space of XX, which is spanned by X​WXW.

Thus, l=‖(I−PX)​Y‖F2l=||(I-P_{X})Y||_{F}^{2}. To relate YY to how it appears in CCA’s similarity index, note that each of its columns is a vector in its column space. Intuitively, if q1,…,qp1q_{1},...,q_{p_{1}} is an orthonormal basis for YY’s column space, then each vector in the column space can be decomposed as y=∑i=1p1(qiT​y)​qiy=\sum_{i=1}^{p_{1}}(q_{i}^{T}y)q_{i}. In matrix form, this gives the identity Y=QY​QYT​YY=Q_{Y}Q^{T}_{Y}Y, with QYQ_{Y} being an orthonormal basis column for YY’s column space. More generally, for any ZZ we have that PZ=QZ​QZTP_{Z}=Q_{Z}Q_{Z}^{T}, where PZP_{Z} is the projection matrix onto ZZ’s column space and QZQ_{Z} is a matrix of that space’s orthonormal basis.

Now, note that as ‖A​B‖F2≤‖A‖F2​‖B‖F2||AB||_{F}^{2}\leq||A||_{F}^{2}||B||_{F}^{2}, we have that l=‖(I−PX)​Y‖F2=‖(I−PX)​QY​QYT​Y‖F2l=||(I-P_{X})Y||_{F}^{2}=||(I-P_{X})Q_{Y}Q_{Y}^{T}Y||_{F}^{2}, as QYQ_{Y} acts as the identity on YY. Using the inequality, we have that l≤||(I−PX)​QY||F2​‖QYT​Y‖F2=‖(I−PX)​QY‖F2​‖Y‖F2l\leq||(I-P_{X})Q_{Y}||_{F}^{2}||Q_{Y}^{T}Y||_{F}^{2}=||(I-P_{X})Q_{Y}||_{F}^{2}||Y||_{F}^{2}, with the last step being due to QY​QYTQ_{Y}Q_{Y}^{T} acting as the identity on YY, where ‖QYT​Y‖F2=Tr⁡(YT​QY​QYT​Y)=Tr⁡(YT​Y)=||Y||F2||Q_{Y}^{T}Y||_{F}^{2}=\Tr(Y^{T}Q_{Y}Q_{Y}^{T}Y)=\Tr(Y^{T}Y)=||Y||_{F}^{2}.

We now connect this quantity to CCA. As the Frobenius norm is invariant to orthonormal matrices, note that ‖QXT​QY‖F2=‖QX​QXT​QY‖F2=||PX​QY||F2||Q_{X}^{T}Q_{Y}||_{F}^{2}=||Q_{X}Q_{X}^{T}Q_{Y}||_{F}^{2}=||P_{X}Q_{Y}||_{F}^{2}. We now note that this is the complementary part of a projection term that bounds ll, namely the ‖(I−PX)​QY‖F2||(I-P_{X})Q_{Y}||_{F}^{2} term. Thus, using Pythagoras’ theorem, ‖(I−PX)​QY‖F2+‖PX​QY‖F2=‖QY‖F2≤p1||(I-P_{X})Q_{Y}||_{F}^{2}+||P_{X}Q_{Y}||_{F}^{2}=||Q_{Y}||_{F}^{2}\leq p_{1}, with the last step being due to QYQ_{Y} being an orthonormal column matrix, with the inequality being tight when YY is full rank. Plugging these results together, we have that:

RCCA2=‖QXT​QY‖F2p1=‖QY‖F2−‖(I−PX)​QY‖F2p1≤p1−‖(I−PX)​QY‖F2p1≤1−l‖Y‖F2​p1.R^{2}_{\text{CCA}}=\frac{||Q_{X}^{T}Q_{Y}||_{F}^{2}}{p_{1}}=\frac{||Q_{Y}||_{F}^{2}-||(I-P_{X})Q_{Y}||_{F}^{2}}{p_{1}}\leq\frac{p_{1}-||(I-P_{X})Q_{Y}||_{F}^{2}}{p_{1}}\leq 1-\frac{l}{||Y||_{F}^{2}p_{1}}.

Thus, if the linear alignability is bounded, where l>ε>0l>\varepsilon>0, then RCCA2<1−ε‖Y‖F2​p1R^{2}_{\text{CCA}}<1-\frac{\varepsilon}{||Y||_{F}^{2}p_{1}} is bounded as well. Note that this bound is quite loose and for illustration only, as there are various places in the derivation where it could be made tighter.

Different similarity structures bound CKA. In section 3 we show that if two representations have the same similarity structure then there is a linear mapping between them. Here we expand on what happens when their similarity structures differ; namely, how larger differences between the similarity structures generally lead to lower CKA.

Denote by KX≔X​XT,KY≔Y​YTK_{X}\coloneqq XX^{T},K_{Y}\coloneqq YY^{T} the Gram matrices for XX and YY respectively, which as per definition 3.4 denote each representation’s similarity structure. Denote by K^\hat{K} a normalized Gram matrix, where K^≔K‖K‖F\hat{K}\coloneqq\frac{K}{||K||_{F}}. Thus, a natural scale-invariant notion for the difference between two similarity structures is d≔‖K^Y−KX^‖F2d\coloneqq||\hat{K}_{Y}-\hat{K_{X}}||_{F}^{2}. Linking this to CKA, note that Tr⁡(K^YT​K^X)=Tr⁡(KYT​KX)‖KY‖F​‖KX‖F=CKA​(X,Y)\Tr(\hat{K}_{Y}^{T}\hat{K}_{X})=\frac{\Tr(K_{Y}^{T}K_{X})}{||K_{Y}||_{F}||K_{X}||_{F}}=\text{CKA}(X,Y). Thus, by expanding dd we find that d=‖K^Y‖F2+‖K^X‖F2−2​Tr⁡(K^YT​K^X)=2​(1−CKA​(X,Y))d=||\hat{K}_{Y}||_{F}^{2}+||\hat{K}_{X}||_{F}^{2}-2\Tr(\hat{K}_{Y}^{T}\hat{K}_{X})=2(1-\text{CKA}(X,Y)).

Thus, if the difference between the normalized similarity structures is bounded, so d>εd>\varepsilon, the CKA between them is bounded as well, where CKA​(X,Y)<1−ε2\text{CKA}(X,Y)<1-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.

Appendix C Proofs of Theorems

We restate the theorems here for convenience. We believe essentially all of our theorems have standard linear algebra versions that are generally known but we did not find a source for some, so we provide short proofs for them instead. For ease of notation we drop the concepts in the notation, so vXi=viv_{X_{i}}=v_{i}. We first prove Theorem 3.7 as Theorem 3.5’s proof relies on it, it being the weaker of the two.

Theorem 3.7 (Generalized analogies enable linear mappings.) Let VV and WW have corresponding sets of concept representations, {vi}i=1N\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and {wi}i=1N\{w_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}. A linear map TT such that ∀i:T⁡(vi)=wi\forall i:T(v_{i})=w_{i} exists if and only if for all sets of scalars ai∈ℝa_{i}\in\mathbb{R} if ∑iai​vi=0\sum_{i}a_{i}v_{i}=0 then ∑iai​wi=0\sum_{i}a_{i}w_{i}=0.

Proof. It is simple to see that having such a TT is sufficient, as ∑i=1Nai​vi=0⇒T⁡(∑i=1Nai​vi)=T⁡(0)=0\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}v_{i}=0\Rightarrow T(\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}v_{i})=T(0)=0, and due to linearity T⁡(∑i=1Nai​vi)=∑i=1Nai​T​(vi)=∑i=1Nai​wiT(\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}v_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}T(v_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}w_{i}, which completes this part of the proof.

As for necessity, assume that ∀ai∈ℝ:∑i=1Nai​vi=0⇒∑i=1Nai​wi=0\forall a_{i}\in\mathbb{R}:\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}v_{i}=0\Rightarrow\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}w_{i}=0. We prove this using induction on NN, the number of vectors. For the base case this is trivial, as only for a1=0a_{1}=0 the statement holds and the map ∀a∈ℝ:T⁡(a​v1)=a​w1\forall a\in\mathbb{R}:T(av_{1})=aw_{1} is clearly a valid linear transformation. For induction, assume the statement holds for N−1N-1 and we wish to show it for NN. If vNv_{N} is linearly dependent on {vi}i=1N−1\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N-1} then ∃ai∈ℝ:vN=∑i=1N−1ai​vi\exists a_{i}\in\mathbb{R}:v_{N}=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}a_{i}v_{i}, so −vN+∑i=1N−1ai​vi=0⇒−wN+∑i=1N−1ai​wi=0⇒wN=∑i=1N−1ai​wi-v_{N}+\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}a_{i}v_{i}=0\Rightarrow-w_{N}+\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}a_{i}w_{i}=0\Rightarrow w_{N}=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}a_{i}w_{i}. Thus, as T⁡(∑i=1N−1ai​vi)=T⁡(vN)=wNT(\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}a_{i}v_{i})=T(v_{N})=w_{N} the same linear transformation works here as well.

If vNv_{N} is linearly independent of {vi}i=1N−1\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N-1} then recall that for two vector spaces V,WV,W there exists a linear transformation between a basis of VV and any set of vectors in WW. Assume without loss of generality that {vi}i=1N−1\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N-1} are linearly independent, as otherwise a vector could be removed from the set without altering its span and the induction hypothesis could readily be used with the reduced set and vNv_{N}. Thus, the set {vi}i=1N\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} is linearly independent and the aforementioned lemma can be used for V′≔span⁡({vi}i=1N)V^{\prime}\coloneqq\operatorname{span}(\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}) and WW. Therefore, such a TT exists. If V′⊂VV^{\prime}\subset V then TT can be extended to be over VV by mapping basis vectors in V/V′V/V^{\prime} to 0, thereby completing the proof. ∎

Theorem 3.5 (Same similarities enable linear mappings.) Let VV and WW have corresponding sets of concept representations, {vi}i=1N\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and {wi}i=1N\{w_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}. If ∀i,j:viT​vj=wiT​wj\forall i,j:v_{i}^{T}v_{j}=w_{i}^{T}w_{j} then there exists a linear map T:V→WT:V\to W such that ∀i:T⁡(vi)=wi\forall i:T(v_{i})=w_{i}.

Proof. We wish to show that ∀ai∈ℝ:∑iai​vi=0⇒∑iai​wi=0\forall a_{i}\in\mathbb{R}:\sum_{i}a_{i}v_{i}=0\Rightarrow\sum_{i}a_{i}w_{i}=0, thus allowing us to use Theorem 3.7. Let there be some set of aia_{i} such that ∑iai​vi=0\sum_{i}a_{i}v_{i}=0. Multiplying by ∑iai​vi\sum_{i}a_{i}v_{i} and using that viT​vj=wiT​wjv_{i}^{T}v_{j}=w_{i}^{T}w_{j}, we have that ‖∑iai​vi‖2=∑i,jai​aj​viT​vj=∑i,jai​aj​wiT​wj=0\|\sum_{i}a_{i}v_{i}\|^{2}=\sum_{i,j}a_{i}a_{j}v_{i}^{T}v_{j}=\sum_{i,j}a_{i}a_{j}w_{i}^{T}w_{j}=0. Note that ∑i,jai​aj​wiT​wj=‖∑iai​wi‖2=0\sum_{i,j}a_{i}a_{j}w_{i}^{T}w_{j}=\|\sum_{i}a_{i}w_{i}\|^{2}=0, and as ∑iai​wi\sum_{i}a_{i}w_{i} is of length zero it must be the zero vector. Thus, ∑iai​wi=0\sum_{i}a_{i}w_{i}=0 and the proof is complete. ∎

It is easy to see that the resulting transformation T⁡(vi)=wiT(v_{i})=w_{i} is an isometry over span⁡({vi})\operatorname{span}(\{v_{i}\}) as ∀ai∈ℝ:‖∑i=1Nai​vi‖2=∑i​j=1Nai​aj​viT​vj\forall a_{i}\in\mathbb{R}:\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}v_{i}\|^{2}=\sum_{ij=1}^{N}a_{i}a_{j}v_{i}^{T}v_{j} so due to the sets of concepts having the same similarity structure this equals ∑i​j=1Nai​aj​wiT​wj=‖∑i=1Nai​wi‖2=‖∑i=1nai​T​(vi)‖2=‖T⁡(∑i=1Nai​vi)‖2\sum_{ij=1}^{N}a_{i}a_{j}w_{i}^{T}w_{j}=\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}w_{i}\|^{2}=\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}T(v_{i})\|^{2}=\|T(\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}v_{i})\|^{2}, so distances are preserved. The corollary, where different similarity structures rule out there being an isometry between the representations, is straightforward to prove:

Corollary 3.6(Different similarity structures rule out isometric mappings) Assume V,WV,W have corresponding sets of concept representations but different similarity structures. Thus, there cannot exist an isometric linear map T:V→WT:V\to W such that ∀i:T⁡(vXi)=wXi\forall i:T(v_{X_{i}})=w_{X_{i}}.

Proof.

Assume for the sake of contradiction that there exists such an isometric linear map. As TT is an isometry and thus respects inner products, ∀i,j:vXiT​vXj=T​(vXi)T​T​(vXj)=wXiT​wXj\forall i,j:v_{X_{i}}^{T}v_{X_{j}}=T(v_{X_{i}})^{T}T(v_{X_{j}})=w_{X_{i}}^{T}w_{X_{j}}. However, as the two representations have a different similarity structure, ∃i,j:vXiT​vXj≠wXiT​wXj\exists i,j:v_{X_{i}}^{T}v_{X_{j}}\not=w_{X_{i}}^{T}w_{X_{j}}, thereby yielding a contradiction and completing the proof. ∎

Appendix F Small-Scale Experiments Details

For captioning, a linear layer is trained between the vision and language models as an adapter. For retrieval each has a linear layer trained on top of its last layer representations, by default using the class token for the vision head and averaging the post-adapter token representations for the language model. Different, more powerful adapters and representation aggregation schemes were not found to make a big difference. The training data is COCO-2014 (Lin et al., 2014).

To ensure the models are well trained optimal learning rates and weight decays were chosen by doing a grid search over learning rates and weight decays, spaced log-linearly in 10−5,10−4.5,…​10−210^{-5},10^{-4.5},...10^{-2} and 10−4,10−3,…​10−110^{-4},10^{-3},...10^{-1} respectively. Optimal retrieval hyperparameters were chosen based on the model’s top-1 ImageNet classification accuracy over ImageNet’s validation set. Generation hyperparameters were optimized on the BLEU score over COCO’s validation set. Models were trained for 10 epochs with an early stopping patience of 5, with validation metrics computed once every 0.25 epochs.

Resulting optimal hyperparameters for all generative model configurations, including those referenced in the next section, are listed in Table 3. For retrieval a learning rate of 10−410^{-4} and weight decay of 10−210^{-2} was found to work well for all settings.

F.1 Different Adapters Yield Similar Results

To see if better adapters help we repeated the two small-scale experiments with two more powerful adapters – an MLP and an attention block between the tokens and learnable embeddings. The attention adapter has a single learnable token embedding for retrieval and 200 learnable embeddings for generation, where a ViT-B/16 has 197 vision tokens by default. For retrieval we also experiment with three different kinds of pooling – mean pooling, max pooling, and, specifically for the vision transformer, taking the class token. When the vision transformer uses the class token the language model defaults to mean pooling. The attention adapter needs no pooling due to the cross attention already aggregating information.

All adapters and choices of pooling yielded similar held-out concept detection accuracies. At the end of training, the models trained without the held-out concepts have detection rates of 1.2%, 2.0% and 2.2% of the time with the linear, MLP and attention adapters respectively. The retrieval models reach concept detection accuracies between 1.6% and 8.9%, with a linear adapter and max pooling doing best. When trained on the full dataset, all generative variants reach 84.0–85.9% and all retrieval variants 79.0–81.5%. Even the best held-out concept detection accuracy at any point during training, a much more lenient metric, remains low: 7.2% for generation and 10.3% for retrieval, both with a linear adapter. Held-out concept accuracies are averaged over concepts and measured every 0.1 epochs.

Appendix G What Does it Mean for a Model to “Know” of a Concept?

For the vision models this is simple – all the concepts are ImageNet classes and the models are ImageNet classifiers that get high accuracies. For the language models, they can be prompted to complete texts such as “a <concept> is” or asked questions about it, thereby gauging some form of recognition.

To see whether the LLaVA backbone knows of the held-out concepts we ask it various questions about them, such as “What is a zebra?” and “What is a horse-like animal with black and white stripes?”. Doing so with the LLaVA model’s LLM backbone after it was trained showed that the language model by itself still recognizes the held-out concepts.

Appendix H Concept Filtering

The held-out concepts are “zebra”, “banana”, “pizza”, “umbrella”, and “toothbrush” for the small-scale experiments, with additionally “broccoli”, “microwave”, “strawberry”, “castle”, “envelope”, “violin”, “tractor”, “flamingo”, “printer”, “volcano” for the large-scale experiments. The small-scale experiments use a smaller concept set as even the small scale models trained on the entire dataset fail to detect most of the additional concepts. To ensure the datasets are not overly reduced, for the large-scale experiments we train three models without the held-out concepts, each having only five concepts held-out.

To filter the held-out concepts from the finetuning data we remove all image-text pairs where a) the text contains the object’s name or b) the image is likely to contain it. Image-based filtering is important to prevent misclassified data from hampering the experiment, e.g. zebra images accidentally captioned as giraffes. This is done using a CLIP ViT-L/14 model and filtering images with a similarity above a chosen threshold to the text “a photo of a <concept>”, with the threshold found through manual tuning. For the small-scale experiments the threshold was 0.2 while for the large-scale ones it was 0.25. This reduces the datasets by at most 9%.

Specifically for the large-scale experiment we also filter the concepts “tooth brush” and “volcanic” as we find they are occasionally not detected by the image-based filter. There may be other, less direct forms of leakage we are unaware of that artificially boost the large-scale model’s performance on detecting held-out concepts.

See Figure 8. Note that all descriptions are generated at T=0T=0, except for the successful banana example (o), as none of the T=0T=0 descriptions of the banana images mention a banana. Example (o) was obtained by sampling with T=0.2T=0.2 repeatedly.

Appendix J Discussion on Large-Scale Results

The large-scale model getting better held-out concept detection accuracies than the smaller models could mean that the failure described in Section 4 is partially alleviated by scale. However, there are other possible reasons a larger model could do better, such as LLaVA generally outputting longer completions or it potentially relying on its internal knowledge more so than what it sees, akin to the failure described by Vo et al. (2025). For example, the completion of “a bathroom with a toilet, mirror, toothpaste, …” would likely mention a toothbrush regardless of whether it actually exists in the image.

To test this, we benchmark the large-scale models when prompting them to only name the main object they see in the image, limiting them to output answers with at most 8 tokens. In this setting the models trained without the held-out concepts performed comparably well, getting an average detection accuracy of 19.6%. Thus, the large-scale model’s success is not due to relying on the language model’s knowledge while ignoring the vision model.

Another option is that there is some data leakage. While running these experiments, we initially filtered for “toothbrush” but not for “tooth brush”, thereby having some examples slip by. As larger models are more sample efficient, these ∼\sim20 extra image-text pairs resulted in toothbrushes being detected much more often. In the current setup, the large-scale models detect “pizza” much more than any other concept, although it is hard to say whether there is some data leakage we have not managed to find, the better detection performance is due to scale, or some mixture thereof. When training the model with the dataset visual similarity filtering threshold set to 0.2 instead of 0.25 models generally perform much worse, getting accuracies around half of those reported in Table 2, which lends credence to there possibly being some leakage.

Appendix K Details on Section 5 LLaVA Models

For the vision backbones we use 11 different standard pretrained ViT-B models and 26 finetunes thereof. ViT-B are used and not ViT-L, which is more typical for LLaVA, due to not all models having pretrained ViT-L variants. For the original set of 11 models, we use BEiT (Bao et al., 2021), CLIP models trained by OpenAI and on the Datacomp dataset (Radford et al., 2021; Gadre et al., 2023), DEiT (Touvron et al., 2021), DINO (Caron et al., 2021), DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2023), MAE (He et al., 2022), SIGLip and SIGLip2 (Zhai et al., 2023; Tschannen et al., 2025), and ViTs trained on ImageNet 1k and 21k (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020). For the 26 finetunes we use 6 models from FusionBench (Tang et al., 2025) and various other models uploaded to HuggingFace, all with at least 400 downloads over the last month as of writing (Nurul, 2023; Iakubovskyi, 2023a; Iakubovskyi, 2023b; Iakubovskyi, 2023c; Iakubovskyi, 2023d; Iakubovskyi, 2023e; Enright, 2023; Ng, 2023; Vishwakarma, 2023; Sharma, 2024a; Sharma, 2024b; Sharma, 2024c; Iakubovskyi, 2024a; Iakubovskyi, 2024b; Dark Coder, 2025; Sakthi, 2025b; prithivMLmods, 2025; Sakthi, 2025a; Sakthi, 2025c; Abhilash, 2025).

Appendix L Limitations

Representational similarity is generally a vague notion without a universally agreed upon definition, making it difficult to making decisive claims on representational similarity or alignability (Sucholutsky et al., 2023). While we attempt to make broad claims by showing connections between different measures of similarity (see section 2) and grounding results in theory where possible (section 3), these are naturally not exhaustive over the many notions of similarity. Additionally, results are believed to be general due to their underlying cause, namely inherent differences in the information content in different modalities. The difference in information content has been discussed in several prior works (Gal, 2021; Schrodi et al., 2025), with the results herein providing further evidence.

Most of the theoretical results are on linear alignability while in practice many VLMs are built using nonlinear adapters. Some results show that linear alignability bounds some notions of nonlinear similarity between representations (Appendix B), while others show that failures appear also given nonlinear alignment, namely the LLaVA experiments in sections 4 and 5, and the ablations in Appendix F.1.

Most results are circumstantial in supporting that many VLM failures likely arise due to representational misalignment. In this sense the results are consistent with the hypothesis but do not causally show that representational misalignment is what caused a failure. Results in section 4 are an important exception, as based on the theory they make a causal prediction which turns out to be correct – that if vision-language representations are misaligned then the generalization failure would occur.
